analysis.one_liner: Bans forced arbitration clauses buried in consumer contracts, restoring consumers' right to sue in court.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 2007 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never acted on it; it died without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies routinely write clauses into cell phone, credit card, loan, and other standard contracts that force customers to settle disputes in private arbitration instead of court, often before the customer has even seen the fine print. This bill would make such clauses unenforceable and an unfair trade practice under federal law. Customers could still choose arbitration freely after a dispute actually arises, but companies could not force it in advance. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who signs a standard consumer contract — credit card holders, borrowers, renters, cell phone and service customers — would regain the ability to take a dispute to court instead of a private arbitration forum chosen by the company. Consumers as a class also gain by deterring practices that are easier to commit when lawsuits are blocked.

how_it_helps.text: The bill treats any written clause requiring binding arbitration in a consumer transaction as an unfair and deceptive trade practice that cannot be enforced.
It covers the full range of consumer dealings: sales, rentals, credit extensions, and financial products or services signed for personal, family, or household purposes.
It preserves consumer choice by allowing binding arbitration for an existing dispute if both sides agree in writing after the controversy has arisen.
It applies to new contracts and amendments after enactment, and to controversies pending or arising after enactment, so companies could not keep old clauses alive.

analysis.who_pays: Banks, credit card issuers, lenders, cell phone and service providers, and other businesses that use standard-form arbitration clauses would lose a shield that limits costly class-action lawsuits and keeps disputes out of public courts. The arbitration industry would lose a large flow of mandatory case referrals.
analysis.who_pays_short: Lenders and firms using arbitration clauses

drawbacks.text: Businesses argue arbitration is faster and cheaper than court for many small claims, and that class actions often deliver little to individual class members while enriching lawyers — a trade-off this bill would not address.

A blanket ban reaches nearly every consumer contract in the country, and some parties might prefer arbitration in particular cases; the bill responds by permitting arbitration only after a dispute arises, which is narrower than allowing it by mutual agreement up front.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and large: consumers would get their day in court, and companies could no longer bury the loss of that right in fine print. The cost to businesses of returning disputes to public courts is genuine, and some consumers might have chosen arbitration voluntarily; the bill's after-the-dispute carve-out addresses that but with a blunter instrument than some alternatives. On balance the bill would shift bargaining power sharply toward individual consumers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or vote on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Luis Gutierrez introduced the Consumer Fairness Act of 2007 on March 9, 2007, joined by four Democratic cosponsors: Reps. Jackson-Lee, Kucinich, Gonzalez, and Schakowsky.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
No further action appears in the bill's history — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — before the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks, lenders, and other companies that write arbitration clauses into standard contracts are better off; the bill died, so their arbitration shield stays intact and consumers remain without a practical route to court.

for.name: Rep. Luis Gutierrez
for.role: Sponsor, House Financial Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban unilaterally imposed consumer arbitration clauses.

for.name: Reps. Jackson-Lee, Kucinich, Gonzalez, and Schakowsky

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.role: Committee of referral under Chairman Barney Frank (D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markups on the bill; it sat without action until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; the committee that buried it was chaired by a fellow Democrat, and no Republican supported the bill in the record.

industries.industry: Banks, credit card issuers, and consumer lenders
industries.note: These companies rely on arbitration clauses in credit card and loan contracts to push disputes into private forums and block class-action lawsuits. The bill would strip that shield, restoring consumers' ability to sue in court.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers and private dispute-resolution firms
industries.note: Mandatory arbitration clauses channel a steady stream of consumer disputes to private arbitrators for fees. A ban on unilateral clauses would cut off much of that mandatory business, leaving only post-dispute voluntary agreements.

industries.industry: Telecom, retail, and other standard-contract sellers
industries.note: Any business selling goods or services through standardized consumer contracts would lose the ability to force arbitration as a condition of the deal.
